title: The 3n + 1 Problem
subtitle: A rule a child can follow, a question nobody can answer
thesis: One line of arithmetic generates behaviour that outruns every tool we have for proving things about it.
outcomes: Follow the map by hand and read a trajectory
Explain why parity, not algebra, is the wall
State precisely what has been proved — and what has not
Recognise a crank proof when you see one

identity.rationale: hand-worked arithmetic reads best warm, quiet and generously spaced

warnings: M0 build: no source-reading pass ran, so every claim here is model knowledge. Sources and timestamps arrive with the research milestone.

sections.title: A game with two moves
sections.hook: You can learn the whole problem in twenty seconds and spend a lifetime on it.

blocks.md: Pick a whole number. If it is **even**, cut it in half. If it is **odd**, triple it and add one. Now do it again with the number you got. And again.
A game with exactly two moves, decided by one question: *odd or even?* You never choose. The number chooses.

Start with 6: it halves to 3, then 3 becomes 10, 10 halves to 5, 5 becomes 16, 16 halves to 8, 8 to 4, 4 to 2, 2 to 1. Eight moves to reach 1.

Now the question that breaks mathematics: does **every** starting number eventually reach 1?

Define a function on the positive integers: **T(n) = n/2** when n is even, and **T(n) = 3n + 1** when n is odd. The sequence *n, T(n), T²(n), …* is the **trajectory** of n. The Collatz conjecture says every trajectory reaches 1.
The number of steps σ(n) needed to first reach 1. σ(6) = 8, σ(1) = 0. If a trajectory never reaches 1, σ(n) is undefined — and that is exactly the case the conjecture forbids.

Write the map on ℕ⁺ as a single expression using the parity indicator: **T(n) = (3n + 1)·[n odd] + (n/2)·[n even]**. Nothing about it is exotic — it is a piecewise-linear map with two branches, integer coefficients, and no free parameters.
T(n) = (3n + 1)/2 when n ≡ 1 (mod 2),  n/2 when n ≡ 0 (mod 2)

Most of the literature uses the **accelerated** form, which folds the forced halving that follows an odd step into the same move: T'(n) = (3n + 1)/2 for odd n, n/2 for even n. Trajectories agree up to reindexing; stopping times differ by a bounded amount. That the map is cheap to state and cheap to compute is the whole trap — it looks like something a proof should fall out of.

exercise.prompt: You start at 7. What is the next term?
exercise.why: 7 is odd, so the odd branch applies: 3 × 7 + 1 = 22. (Twenty-one is 3 × 7 — the step everyone forgets to finish.)

sections.title: Hailstones
sections.hook: Numbers that climb before they fall, and one small number that refuses to behave.

blocks.md: Watch a number climb instead of fall. Start at 27 and it goes up to 82, then 41, then 124… and keeps bouncing for a hundred steps before it finally lands on 1. Up and down like a hailstone in a storm — that is what people called these sequences.
27 is the famous one because it is so small and takes so long: **111 steps**, and on the way it reaches **9,232** — more than three hundred times where it started.

Trajectories are not monotone and they are not random either. σ(n) grows slowly and very irregularly: σ(27) = 111, while σ(97) = 118 and σ(871) = 178. Records keep getting broken at unpredictable values, which is one reason statistical arguments are so hard to make rigorous.

blocks.caption: The trajectory of 27 on a logarithmic vertical axis: 111 steps, peaking at 9,232. The sawtooth is the parity of the current number — odd steps jump, even steps fall.

blocks.md: You should now be able to say what a trajectory is, what σ(n) counts, and why a small starting value can produce a long one.

Model a trajectory by its **parity vector** — the sequence of odd/even decisions along the way. Under a uniform-random model of that vector, the multiplier after k odd and 2k even steps is 3^k / 2^{2k} = (3/4)^k, which decays geometrically. So the heuristic expectation is drift toward 0, plus rare enormous excursions — exactly the hailstone picture.
E[log T(n)] ≈ (1/2)log 3 − log 2 < 0
The gap between that expectation and a theorem is the entire problem: the parity decisions are not independent, and no known technique converts a heuristic drift into a statement about every integer.

exercise.prompt: In your own words: why is 27 the example everyone uses?
exercise.answer: Because it is a small starting value with an unusually long and high trajectory: 111 steps, rising to 9,232 before collapsing to 1. It is the cheapest possible counterexample to the intuition that small numbers behave modestly.

sections.title: Parity eats algebra
sections.hook: The one question the rule asks is the one question algebra cannot see.

blocks.md: Here is the difficulty in one sentence: the rule asks *is it odd or even?*, and that question has no clean answer in the language we use for equations.
A recipe that says "if the egg is fresh, do this; otherwise do that". Perfectly clear instructions — but if all you have is a shopping list, the freshness test is invisible.

Algebraic arguments want a quantity that always grows, always shrinks, or stays fixed. The Collatz map has none: it multiplies by 3 and adds 1 on half its inputs and divides by 2 on the other half, and which branch you take depends on a property (parity) that is not preserved under the operations involved.
There is no known invariant, no known monotone, and no known embedding into a dynamical system where the question becomes easy. Every "proof" that circulates fails at exactly this point.

The first k parity decisions determine n modulo 2^k, and that determines everything up to an affine map: after k steps, **T^k(n) = (3^a n + b) / 2^c**, where a is the number of odd steps, c the number of even steps, and b depends on the order of decisions. That is Terras' starting point — the parity vector of length k is a function of n mod 2^k and nothing else.
T^k(n) = (3^a n + b(n)) / 2^c,  with a + c = k

This is also why the problem has a natural 2-adic formulation (Lagarias' conjugacy of T to the shift on ℤ₂): the parity sequence is the base-2 expansion, and the map becomes a shift. It gives a clean dynamical picture without giving a proof.

exercise.prompt: The parity vector of length k is determined by which quantity?
exercise.why: Only n mod 2^k matters for the first k decisions — the rest of n is invisible until later. That is the precise sense in which parity is a 2-adic, not an algebraic, obstruction.

sections.title: What is actually proved
sections.hook: Almost everything works. That is not the same as everything.

blocks.md: We know a lot. Every starting number anyone has ever checked — all of them up to about **295 quintillion** — reaches 1. We also know that if you pick a number at random, the chance it fails is zero in a precise sense.
What we do not know is whether there is one number, somewhere out there, that never lands.

The results cluster into three kinds. **Density results:** Terras (1976) proved that the set of n with finite stopping time has density 1. **Explicit bounds:** Krasikov and Lagarias and successors bound how many n below x can have unusually long trajectories. **Exhaustive verification:** every n < 2^68 has been checked (Barina, 2020).
Then Tao (2019): *almost all* orbits attain *almost bounded* values — a statement about density, not about every integer. It is the strongest result of its kind and it still does not say "all".

blocks.title: The word doing all the work
blocks.md: "Almost all" means the exceptions form a set of density zero. Density zero is not empty: the perfect squares have density zero, and there are infinitely many of them. Any argument that slides from *almost all* to *all* is not a proof, and it is the most common error in amateur attempts.

Precisely: Terras showed that the set of n whose trajectory reaches a value below n (finite *stopping time*, not total stopping time) has natural density 1. Tao proved that for any function f tending to infinity, the set of n whose orbit attains a value below f(n) has density 1. Neither statement excludes an exceptional set of density zero, and the conjecture is exactly the claim that this exceptional set is empty.

exercise.prompt: "Almost all integers reach 1" — what does that assert?
choices: All but a set of density zero reach 1
exercise.why: Density one is a statement about proportions below x as x grows, not about membership. An infinite exceptional set of density zero is perfectly compatible with it.

sections.title: Cycles
sections.hook: A trajectory can fail in two ways, and one of them is much better studied.

blocks.md: There are two ways to never reach 1: fly off to infinity, or go round in a loop. Loops are easier to rule out, and people have ruled out all the small ones — but not all of them.

The trivial loop 1 → 4 → 2 → 1 is the only cycle anyone has found. Every other cycle has been excluded up to enormous lengths — Eliahou's 1993 argument rules out cycles shorter than about seventeen million steps — by turning the existence of a cycle into a Diophantine equation and bounding its solutions.

items: Continued fractions and Diophantine bounds apply

blocks.md: n(2^c − 3^a) = b  where a = #odd steps, c = #even steps, b > 0

A cycle with a odd and c even steps returns to its start, so n·2^c = 3^a·n + b, i.e. n = b/(2^c − 3^a). Since 2^c and 3^a are never equal for positive a, c, the denominator is nonzero — and the whole question becomes how well 3^a/2^c can approximate 1 while keeping b small. That is a Diophantine approximation problem, and it is where the real bounds come from.

For a putative cycle, the linear relation above forces 2^c − 3^a to divide b, with b determined by the pattern of parity decisions. Eliahou (1993) combined this with continued-fraction convergents of log₂3 to exclude cycle lengths below 17,087,915; later work extended the range. These arguments are rigorous but conditional on the cycle's shape — they say nothing about divergence.

items: 2019 — Tao: almost bounded values for almost all orbits

exercise.prompt: A cycle with a odd and c even steps must satisfy which relation?
exercise.why: Returning to the start means n·2^c = 3^a·n + b. Rearranged: n(2^c − 3^a) = b. Since 3^a ≠ 2^c, the term in brackets is nonzero — which is what makes the problem Diophantine rather than impossible.

sections.title: Why the heuristic is not a proof
sections.hook: The random-walk argument is convincing, correct in spirit, and completely insufficient.

blocks.md: If you pretend each step is a coin flip, the numbers drift downward, so everything should land. That reasoning is why nobody expects a counterexample. It is also not a proof — pretending is not proving.

items: Assume the odd/even pattern behaves like fair coin flips
Compute the average multiplicative drift — it is downward
Conclude that trajectories should almost surely fall to 1
Notice the conclusion is about *typical* numbers, not *every* number
Notice the assumption was never justified

blocks.md: The flaw is not the arithmetic, it is the independence. Parity decisions in a Collatz trajectory are strongly correlated: after an odd step the next value is even by construction, so decisions cannot be treated as independent coin flips. Every attempt to make the heuristic rigorous runs into this.

What would count as progress? A proof that no divergent orbit exists. A proof that no non-trivial cycle exists. A new invariant that constrains all orbits. Or a technique that converts density statements into membership statements — the last one would be a major result in its own right, well beyond this problem.

blocks.caption: Total stopping times for n = 1…60. Spiky, unsmooth, and full of local records — the visual reason why "it grows slowly on average" is not a statement you can prove by looking.

blocks.md: Formally, the heuristic model assigns a probability space of parity sequences and shows the resulting random variable is finite almost surely. A proof of the conjecture would require the actual deterministic orbit to realise a set of sequences that the model calls generic — and there is no known way to establish that an individual integer's parity vector is generic in the required sense, nor any ergodic theorem that applies to the map on ℕ⁺ with counting measure.

blocks.title: How to tell a crank proof in thirty seconds
blocks.md: It proves something strictly stronger than anyone else could (all orbits, all cycles, and usually Goldbach too). It never uses the fact that 3^a and 2^c are multiplicatively independent. It treats the parity sequence as random. And it never states where the density-zero exceptional set went.

exercise.prompt: What exactly is missing between the random-walk heuristic and a proof?
exercise.answer: The heuristic assumes the odd/even decisions are independent coin flips and concludes something about typical orbits. A proof needs the actual orbit of every integer to be typical — but parity decisions are correlated by construction, the counting measure is not ergodic for this map, and a density statement never excludes a density-zero exceptional set.
